newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Pemex needs extra oil output hike in '97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pemex needs extra oil output hike in '97.

text.p: An estimated 9.5 percent increase in Mexico's crude oil output in 1996 over 1995 is a promising advance, but still only slight progress considering the country's potential, according to industry analysts.

"Mexico has not committed the E&P (exploration and production) to the industry the way Venezuela has and Mexico should. Mexico is investing half the resources of Venezuela, so there is no way it can keep up," said Rafael Quijano, director for Latin America at Washington D.C.-based Petroleum Finance Corp.
He suggested Mexico follow the more aggressive example of rival Latin America producer Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA) and aim for an output of six to seven million barrels per day (bpd) in 10 years.

Venezuela's oil firm, unlike Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex), recently reversed its policy on foreign investment and now spurs its E&P spending by allowing private companies to invest in all areas of PdVSA's production.
PdVSA has said it expects at least 10 percent of its income for the next 10 years to come from private companies, as part of profit-sharing agreements.

Mexico's government has ruled out, at least in the short term, attempting to lift the constitutional ban on private capital investing in E&P, in place since 1938, and is financially constrained from additionally boosting output, analysts said.
Pemex estimates 1996 average oil production at 2.86 million bpd, with 1997 levels expected reach 3.08 million bpd.

Venezuela's 1996 oil production potential, estimated by Venezuelan Energy and Mines Minister Erwin Arrieta at an average of 3.2 million bpd, appears to have surpassed Mexico's levels last year and is expected to keep on climbing.
Venezuela, a charter member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), is frequently accused of producing over its 2.359 million bpd OPEC quota.

In December, PdVSA said it had planned to increase its crude reserves by 2.58 billion barrels in 1997 to 68.18 billion barrels. At current production rates using current technology, expected depletion is expected to occur in about 55 years.
Mexico's reserves are reported at 48.8 billion barrels, implying petroleum would be exhausted in about 47 years at current production, according to Mexico's Energy Ministry.

Despite higher output expectations and Pemex's lofty boost to 1997 E&P spending, a budgeted $5.916 billion compared with $3.54 billion in 1996, analysts agreed the company needs more ambitious plans for exploiting Mexico's oil and gas resources.

"Pemex's first, second and third most important priorities (for 1997) should be to increase production," said George Grayson, a government professor and Mexico expert at Virginia's William and Mary College.

"Director general (Adrian) Lajous has made important strides in persuading the government to increase the company's exploration and production budget, but this is only a beginning of where Mexico should be."
Grayson said Mexico ought to be producing at least five million bpd within five years.

"Few new oil discoveries were reported in 1996, but there was news in November of one relatively important new offshore light crude oil field, known as Manik," local energy columnist David Shields wrote recently.
Pemex also plans to invest about $950 million in 1997 as part of a four-year project to expand its most lucrative oil field, Cantarell.

Greater autonomy for the state-owned oil and gas monopoly could help Pemex charge ahead with output expansion goals, Quijano said. More independence is "long overdue," he added, saying the Finance Ministry does not want to relinquish control over its key income source.

The corporation has been pushing to free itself from the administrative grasp of the federal government, which takes almost two-thirds of Pemex's crude export income, expected to reach about $10.7 billion for 1996, according to Shields.
Pemex's Lajous and Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles have reiterated that more autonomous administration of the company is a priority and is being negotiated with the ministry.
Lajous, who recently completed two years as Pemex chief, was credited by many analysts with raising output and spending and improving government relations.
He is the first chairman of Pemex in recent history not to rise from the government political rank and file but from within the oil industry.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7903))
